inputs.root_cause: Following event 164's exact_next_action (XLIFF-SEC-001's 5-fact security baseline is the most promising unstarted lead, now backed by two concrete precedents -- ubl's and nrrd's security findings -- suggesting source-level empirical investigation would be productive), investigated all 5 XLIFF-SEC-001 obligations, all still sharing one generic 3-test citation from event 154 onward.
inputs.obligation_targeted: 5 obligations in XLIFF-SEC-001 -- see the XLIFF-SEC-CITATION-AUDIT-SELECTOR-PROOF execution_evidence entry.
inputs.acceptance_evidence: 3 promoted to implemented (2 via existing but never-individually-cited test coverage, 1 via 5 new tests); 1 stays honestly partial; 1 stays honestly missing.

execution_steps: 1. Read all 5 XLIFF-SEC-001 rule_texts and found them near-identical in shape to UBL-SEC-001's 5 facts (already resolved this session, event 162): network/execution/plugin prevention, untrusted-payload handling, configurable limits with safe defaults, algorithmic-complexity guards, path-traversal prevention.

2. Searched for a dedicated xliff security test file (none found) and read test_production_namespace.py's existing tests directly: found test_dtd_and_entity_declarations_are_rejected (DTD/entity/XXE rejection, already proven) and test_resource_limits_apply_before_xml_processing (a bare max_input_bytes check), but no nesting-depth or node-count rejection test, and no test proving the DEFAULT limits object itself gets enforced when the caller passes none.

3. Read reader.py directly and confirmed _enforce_tree_limits already calls limits.enforce('max_xml_nodes', ...) and limits.enforce('max_nesting_depth', ...) on every parse, and effective_limits() already falls back to XLIFF_DEFAULT_LIMITS -- the enforcement mechanism was real and wired in, just never exercised by a dedicated test. Confirmed interactively (constructing a 50-level-deep document against a tight max_nesting_depth=5 limit) that ResourceLimitError propagates correctly before writing any test.

4. Wrote tests/python/xliff/test_obligation_security_limits.py (5 tests: baseline document loads within default nesting, configured nesting-depth limit rejects, configured node-count limit rejects, effective_limits(None) returns the real default object with positive fields, and a document just over the DEFAULT nesting limit -- not a custom one -- is rejected with no limits argument passed at all). Deliberately avoided constructing a 64MB payload to test the default max_input_bytes (XLIFF_DEFAULT_LIMITS.max_input_bytes is 64MB) since that would be slow and wasteful for a unit test; tested the default-fallback guarantee directly against effective_limits() and the cheaper default-nesting-limit path instead.

5. Ran in isolation (5 passed), ruff clean, full xliff suite (318 passed, was 313, +5, zero regressions). No production source needed changing -- the security machinery already existed and worked, it was purely untested.

6. Checked SAL-XLIFF-OBL-009F2EB91831B248 (path traversal prevention) the same way as the UBL-SEC-001 precedent: grepped the whole xliff model package for path-joining/resolution logic touching untrusted document content, found none -- notes/extensions/original-data references are all opaque stored strings, never dereferenced. Recorded honestly as missing (no attack surface, no test can prove the claim either way) rather than force-promoted, matching the UBL-SEC-001 precedent exactly.

7. Characterized SAL-XLIFF-OBL-130340BC212989D5 (algorithmic complexity/checked arithmetic) as honestly partial: depth/node-count now bounded and tested, but no dedicated complexity-attack-shaped test beyond that exists, and Python's native big-int semantics trivially satisfy 'checked arithmetic' rather than an explicit guarantee -- same characterization as the equivalent already-resolved UBL-SEC-001 obligation.

8. Applied the patch-script pattern. Added the new XLIFF-SEC-CITATION-AUDIT-SELECTOR-PROOF execution_evidence entry, validated the YAML parses (142 total obligations, XLIFF-SEC-001 now 3 implemented / 1 partial / 1 missing), and ran the reconciler.
